title: Organisation and address mapping
summary: Where does an address go? This topic follows an address from the system **address map** through the memory's **fields** — region, bank, word, byte — into rows, columns and banks, and shows how big memories are built from small ones. Interactive diagrams first, then all of it in SystemVerilog.
objectives: Read a system address map and decode an address to a region.
Split a byte address into region, word, bank and byte fields.
Compute address bits and capacity from depth and width.
Explain rows, columns, banks and interleaving and their effect on bandwidth.
Write address decoders and width- and depth-expanded memories in SystemVerilog.

blocks.md: A processor sees **one** address space — 4 GiB for 32-bit addresses. The **address map** divides it into regions: boot ROM, on-chip SRAM, peripheral registers, external DRAM. An **address decoder** looks at the upper address bits and selects the memory that answers; the lower bits are the **offset** inside it. Click the regions:

spots.title: Boot ROM
spots.md: The processor starts executing at address 0 after reset, so the boot code sits there. 64 KiB = 16 offset bits.

spots.title: SRAM
spots.md: Fast on-chip RAM at 0x2000_0000. 128 KiB need 17 offset bits: addr[16:0].

spots.title: APB peripherals
spots.md: Registers of UART, timers, GPIO — accessed like memory (**memory-mapped I/O**) but behind a slower bus.

spots.title: DRAM
spots.md: A large region for external DRAM, reached through a DRAM controller (Topic 9).

spots.title: Address decoder
spots.md: Compares the upper bits with each region. Exactly one region may match; an address in an unmapped hole gives a **bus error** instead of silently reading garbage.

blocks.title: Every memory gets a base address and a size
blocks.md: A region's base address is normally a multiple of its size (aligned). Then the decoder only checks the upper bits, and the lower bits go to the memory unchanged.

subsections.title: From byte address to bank, word and byte

blocks.md: Buses use **byte addresses**: address 0x…04 is the byte after 0x…03. A memory with 32-bit words, however, stores 4 bytes per word, so its **word address** is the byte address without the 2 lowest bits. Follow one address through all its fields:

steps.title: Region
steps.md: addr[31:28] = 0x2 selects the SRAM in the address map.

steps.title: Byte in word
steps.md: addr[1:0] select the byte inside a 32-bit word; for full-word accesses they are 0, for byte writes they choose the byte strobe.

steps.title: Bank
steps.md: In an SRAM with 4 interleaved banks, addr[3:2] — the word address modulo 4 — select the bank.

steps.title: Word in bank
steps.md: The remaining offset bits addr[16:4] address the word inside that bank.

blocks.md:
A memory is described by its **depth** (number of words) and its **width** (bits per word):

> capacity = depth × width  ·  address bits AW = ⌈log₂(depth)⌉

blocks.title: Ki and k
blocks.md: Memory sizes use binary prefixes: 1 Ki = 1024, so 4 KiB = 4096 bytes. Datasheets often write "4 KB" and mean 4096 bytes.

subsections.title: Rows, columns and the column multiplexer

blocks.md: Inside the memory, words are not stored as one long column — the bit lines would be very long and slow. Several words share a **row**, and a **column multiplexer** picks one of them. The word address is split once more:

steps.title: Split the address
steps.md: The high bits select a **row**, the low bits a **column** (a word within the row).

steps.title: Row decoder
steps.md: The decoder raises one of 64 word lines; the whole row — 4 words — is read by the sense amplifiers.

steps.title: Column mux
steps.md: The column bits pick one of the 4 words: here word 2.

blocks.title: Aspect ratio
blocks.md: Memory designers choose rows and columns so that the array is roughly **square**. The column-mux ratio (4:1, 8:1, 16:1) is a parameter of memory compilers.

Large memories are split into **banks** — independent arrays with their own decoders. A bank that is busy with one access cannot start the next; other banks can. **Which address bits select the bank** decides whether consecutive accesses collide:

steps.title: High-order banking
steps.md: The upper address bits select the bank: words 0–3 all live in bank 0.

steps.title: …streaming is slow
steps.md: Reading words 0, 1, 2, 3 hits the same bank four times; each access waits until the previous one is finished.

steps.title: Low-order interleaving
steps.md: The lowest word-address bits select the bank: consecutive words go to consecutive banks.

steps.title: …streaming is fast
steps.md: Four banks work in parallel: a new access every clock.

subsections.title: Building big memories from small ones

steps.title: Width expansion
steps.md: Four 16-bit memories side by side with the **same address** form one 64-bit memory.

steps.title: Depth expansion
steps.md: Four 1K memories with a **decoder** on the upper address bits form one 4K memory; an output mux selects the bank that was read.

blocks.title: Do not forget the registered select
blocks.md: The bank RAMs deliver their data **one clock after** the address. Selecting the output with the *current* bank number instead of the registered one returns the wrong word whenever two consecutive reads go to different banks — a classic bug.

Clock edge: that bank reads its word

subsections.title: In SystemVerilog: organisation and address mapping

blocks.md: **A parameterised single-port RAM** — the building block used from here on:

blocks.code:
module sp_ram #(
  parameter  int DW    = 32,              // width: bits per word
  parameter  int DEPTH = 1024,            // depth: number of words
  localparam int AW    = $clog2(DEPTH)    // address bits
) (
  input  logic          clk,
  input  logic          en,               // access enable
  input  logic          we,               // 1 = write, 0 = read
  input  logic [AW-1:0] addr,
  input  logic [DW-1:0] din,
  output logic [DW-1:0] dout
);
  logic [DW-1:0] mem [DEPTH];             // DEPTH words of DW bits

  always_ff @(posedge clk)
    if (en) begin
      if (we) mem[addr] <= din;
      dout <= mem[addr];                  // read (old value during a write)
    end
endmodule

blocks.md: **An address decoder for the address map** above:

blocks.code:
module addr_decode (
  input  logic [31:0] addr,
  output logic        sel_rom, sel_sram, sel_apb, sel_dram,
  output logic        dec_err              // address not mapped
);
  always_comb begin
    sel_rom  = (addr[31:16] == 16'h0000);  // 0x0000_0000 - 0x0000_FFFF
    sel_sram = (addr[31:17] == 15'h1000);  // 0x2000_0000 - 0x2001_FFFF
    sel_apb  = (addr[31:16] == 16'h4000);  // 0x4000_0000 - 0x4000_FFFF
    sel_dram = (addr[31:30] == 2'b10);     // 0x8000_0000 - 0xBFFF_FFFF
    dec_err  = !(sel_rom || sel_sram || sel_apb || sel_dram);
  end
endmodule

blocks.md: **Splitting the byte address** into the fields of the SRAM:

blocks.code:
logic [31:0] addr;              // byte address from the bus
logic [1:0]  byte_in_word;      // byte strobe select
logic [1:0]  bank;              // 4 banks, interleaved by word
logic [12:0] word_in_bank;      // 8K words per bank

assign byte_in_word = addr[1:0];
assign bank         = addr[3:2];     // word address mod 4
assign word_in_bank = addr[16:4];    // word address div 4
